title: Wind Energy Fundamentals
desc: Learn how wind turbines turn wind into power, how sites are assessed, and the safety, cost and community basics.
outcomes: Explain how a turbine converts wind into electricity.
Estimate energy from wind speed and rotor size.
Judge cost, noise, wildlife and safety.
Write a simple feasibility note for a small wind project.
task: Produce a feasibility note for a small wind installation, with a wind data table, energy estimate, cost and payback, safety and community checks.
condition: A computer, public wind data for a chosen site, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor engineer. No work at height is done in this course.
standard: Energy estimate uses stated formulas and units; payback is calculated in your currency; safety and community points are listed; assumptions are written; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Technicians, engineering students, community energy groups, small farm owners.
evidence: wind data table, energy and payback sheet, safety checklist, feasibility note
modules: How a wind turbine works
Understand
A wind turbine turns the push of moving air into electricity. Knowing the parts and the physics lets you judge any site or machine.
Blades turn a rotor; a generator (with or without a gearbox) makes electricity.
Power in wind = 0.5 x air density x swept area x wind speed cubed, so doubling speed gives eight times the power.
No turbine captures more than about 59 per cent of wind power; real machines reach 35 to 45 per cent.
Turbines start at about 3 m/s, reach rated power near 12 m/s and stop in storms for safety.
A rotor 4 m across sweeps 12.6 square metres. In a 6 m/s wind the air carries 0.5 x 1.2 x 12.6 x 216 = 1,633 W. At 40 per cent the turbine gives about 650 W. At 3 m/s it gives only about 80 W.
Label a turbine diagram and calculate power at 4, 6 and 8 m/s.
Parts are correct; three power values are right and the cube effect is explained in one sentence.
Wind resource and sites
Analyse
Good wind makes or breaks a project, and wind data decides whether to continue.
Use at least one year of data at hub height; short records mislead.
Trees, buildings and hills cause turbulence; put the rotor well above them.
Record average speed, direction and the share of time in each speed band.
Check the distance to the load and to the grid connection.
A hilltop averages 6.5 m/s at 30 m height; a sheltered valley averages 4.2 m/s. The hilltop produces nearly four times the energy from the same turbine.
Tabulate monthly average wind speed for a real or practice site with the data source.
Table has twelve months, units and source.
Estimating energy
Apply
A simple estimate tells you if a project is worth a closer look.
Annual energy = rated power x 8,760 hours x capacity factor.
Small wind capacity factors are often 10 to 25 per cent.
Take the lower value if the data is poor.
Compare with the yearly use of the building.

A 5 kW turbine at 18 per cent capacity factor gives 5 x 8,760 x 0.18 = 7,884 kWh a year. A home using 6,000 kWh a year would cover all of its need over a year; at 10 per cent the output falls to 4,380 kWh.
Estimate yearly energy for low, medium and high capacity factors.
Three results are correct and compared with the user load.
Turbine types and sizes
Analyse
Choose the right size and type for the site and the need.
Horizontal axis machines are common and efficient; vertical axis machines suit gusty, low-height sites but usually produce less.
Match rated power to the load and to the wind speed at the site.
Tower height matters more than a bigger rotor in rough terrain.
Grid-tied and battery-backed designs have different cost and control.
For a farm needing 20 kWh a day, a 3 kW machine at 20 per cent factor gives 14 kWh a day, so a 5 kW machine is the better fit.
Choose a turbine for a given load and site and justify it.
Choice shows size, type, tower height and one reason for each.
Cost and payback
Evaluate
Count the full cost and the full benefit.
Include turbine, tower, foundation, electrical work, permits and labour.
Include maintenance (about 2 to 3 per cent of cost a year) and inverter replacement.
Annual saving = kWh produced x price per kWh.
Payback = cost / annual saving; test weak-wind cases.

A 5 kW system costs 600,000 (an estimate; check your market). It makes 7,884 kWh at 8 per kWh, saving 63,072 a year, less 15,000 maintenance. Net saving 48,072 gives a payback of 12.5 years. At 10 per cent factor payback passes 25 years and the project is not worth it.
Build the cost and payback table for two wind cases.
Costs add up, both cases are shown and a go or no-go is stated.
Safety and maintenance
Apply
Heights, rotating parts and electricity are serious hazards.
Work at height only with training, harness and a rescue plan.
Lock out the turbine and electrical supply before work.
Check bolts, blades, brakes and cables on a schedule.
Keep people clear of blade throw and ice fall zones.
A yearly check finds a loose tower bolt and a cracked blade tip; the turbine is stopped and repaired before it runs again.
Write a one-page maintenance and safety plan.
Plan lists checks, frequency, who does them and stop rules.
Environment and community
Evaluate
Projects work best when neighbours and nature are considered from the start.
Noise, shadow flicker and view concerns need honest discussion.
Check bird and bat routes and apply local rules.
Keep a safe distance from homes and roads, often at least the tower height plus blade length; check the local rule.
Share benefits where possible.
Residents are shown a noise estimate and a map of the safe distance. The turbine is moved 80 m away after they ask.
List four community and nature checks with an action for each.
All four are practical and each has an owner.
Write the feasibility note
Create
Bring it together into a clear decision note.
State the need and the site.
Show the wind table, energy estimate and payback.
Cover safety, permits and community.
End with go, no-go or measure more, with the reason.
The note recommends one more year of measurement because the first-year data covers only seven months.
Write the two-page feasibility note.
All parts are present, numbers agree and the decision is justified.
quiz: What does the generator do?

Turns rotation into electricity. (Covered in module 1: How a wind turbine works. To pass that module: Parts are correct; three power values are right and the cube effect is explained in one sentence.)
What happens to power when wind doubles?
About eight times more. (Covered in module 1: How a wind turbine works. To pass that module: Parts are correct; three power values are right and the cube effect is explained in one sentence.)
Swept area formula?
Pi x radius squared. (Covered in module 1: How a wind turbine works. To pass that module: Parts are correct; three power values are right and the cube effect is explained in one sentence.)
Typical small capacity factor?
10 to 25 percent. (Covered in module 3: Estimating energy. To pass that module: Three results are correct and compared with the user load.)
Name a cost item.
Turbine, tower, foundation, wiring, permits, maintenance. (Covered in module 5: Cost and payback. To pass that module: Costs add up, both cases are shown and a go or no-go is stated.)
Payback formula?
Cost divided by yearly benefit. (Covered in module 5: Cost and payback. To pass that module: Costs add up, both cases are shown and a go or no-go is stated.)
Who may work at height?
Trained, certified people. (Covered in module 6: Safety and maintenance. To pass that module: Plan lists checks, frequency, who does them and stop rules.)
Name two impacts.
Noise and birds (or shadow flicker). (Covered in module 7: Environment and community. To pass that module: All four are practical and each has an owner.)
Why a year of wind data?
To cover all seasons. (Covered in module 2: Wind resource and sites. To pass that module: Table has twelve months, units and source.)
Why decommissioning plan?
To remove and recycle safely. (Covered in module 7: Environment and community. To pass that module: All four are practical and each has an owner.)

Source speeds corrected to hub height, with the uncertainty shown
Planning, noise and wildlife rules for the place are written down
Rules checked with the local authority and a neighbour consulted
